results.question: You receive two Visa card offers: Option A is free but charges 1.5% on every foreign transaction. Option B costs CHF 8/month but has zero foreign fees. You travel to Europe 2–3 times a year. Which do you pick and why?
results.answer: I'd go with the free one honestly. I only travel a few times a year, so 1.5% is probably still cheaper than paying CHF 8 every month. For me, fixed costs hurt more than occasional fees.

results.question: Your bank sends you a message: your free debit card will be replaced by a new Visa card at CHF 5/month. You can opt out and keep a basic account. What do you do?
results.answer: I'd definitely opt out. CHF 5/month is already too much for me if I don't really need it. I'm happy with Twint and my debit card, so I don't see the point.

results.question: A new Visa card offers 1% cashback on all Migros and Coop purchases. The monthly fee is CHF 4. Would this change how you pay at the supermarket?
results.answer: Maybe, but only if the cashback actually beats the CHF 4 fee. I spend quite a bit at Migros and Coop, so it could work, but I'd calculate it first. If it's not clearly saving me money, I'd just stick with Twint.

results.question: Which of these would make you most likely to get a Visa card: (a) 2% cashback, (b) travel insurance included, (c) no foreign transaction fees, (d) a CHF 100 welcome bonus?
results.answer: Honestly (a) 2% cashback. That's something I'd actually use every week, especially for groceries. The others are nice but don't matter much for my daily life.

results.question: You currently use Twint for almost everything. A Visa card promises the same speed but adds rewards. What would it take for you to actually switch?
results.answer: It would need to be free and clearly save me money every month. Like real cashback I can see, not some complicated points system. Otherwise I'll just stay with Twint because it already works perfectly.

results.question: Have you ever been in a situation where Twint or your debit card was not accepted? What did you do — and would a credit card have solved it?
results.answer: Yeah sometimes online or abroad, Twint didn't work. I just used my debit card or skipped it honestly. A credit card might help there, but it's not often enough for me to pay monthly for it.

results.question: A Visa card gives you CHF 50 welcome bonus but requires CHF 6/month for 12 months — total cost CHF 72. Is that a good deal to you?
results.answer: No, that's a bad deal. I'd pay more than I get back, so it doesn't make sense. I'd rather just not get it at all.

results.question: If a Visa card saved you CHF 15/month through cashback and discounts, but cost CHF 10/month in fees, would you see that as a net gain or still feel reluctant?
results.answer: It's a net gain, but I'd still feel a bit hesitant. I'd want to be sure that CHF 15 is realistic every month, not just marketing. If it's consistent, then yeah I'd consider it.

results.question: What is the absolute maximum monthly fee you would accept for a Visa card — and only under what conditions?
results.answer: Max CHF 5, and only if I clearly earn more back than I pay. Like guaranteed cashback on stuff I already buy. Otherwise I just don't see the point.

results.question: If a Visa card were completely free forever but offered no rewards, would you still get one? What would be the point for you?
results.answer: Yeah, I'd probably get it as a backup. For online payments or when Twint doesn't work, it could be useful. But I wouldn't use it much day to day.
